newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - BMW and Mercedes battle over strategies for future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - BMW and Mercedes battle over strategies for future.

text.p: German luxury car makers Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG (BMW) and Mercedes-Benz AG have both seen the future, but they can't agree on how to get there.

The two car makers, mindful of vast overcapacity in the world car market, are expanding their product lines, moving down-market -- well beyond the country club and yuppie sets that have formed the bulk of sales.

But the pair have charted sharply different courses for the future, one through acquisition and the other through internal expansion, and analysts say that will determine who will emerge as the dominant German luxury car maker.

"Both have a proven ability to stay ahead of the game and have strong presences in major markets, but they are following very different routes," said Sabine Bluemel, car industry analyst at IMI Sigeco.

The expansion is being driven by worries about the future of the global market. Car makers worldwide can produce around 70 million cars annually, but most analysts see buyers for only around 50 million.

Analysts say that overcapacity would make it increasingly difficult for relatively small manufacturers, like BMW and Mercedes, which until now have relied on high-income markets -- markets which offer little room for growth.
Although it is too early to say conclusively which company has the upper hand, the risks and profits that each strategy holds are starting to become clearer.
BMW has taken the boldest step, acquiring Rover Group Plc in 1994 in an attempt to move into front-wheel drive cars that cost less than its own up-market models.
The stake was at first greeted as a brilliant move for BMW which at a stroke increased its group annual car production to more than a million, a target that Mercedes also shares.

But with Rover sucking up billions of marks in investment and talk in the automotive industry that transformation of Rover to BMW's own high standards will cost billions more, at least some analysts are starting to question if the deal will pay off.
"The big risk is that Rover could end up being a millstone around BMW's neck," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data. "BMW faces some very difficult decisions."

The motoring media have also carried reports describing friction between German and British staff at Rover with the British company reportedly unwilling to accept its role in the BMW group as a producer of moderately priced cars.
"The Marriage made in Hell," shouted a headline in the September issue of the UK-based "Car Magazine".
BMW denies there is any problem with Rover, saying that the company is developing according to a schedule that will have it making profits by the year 2000.
For its part, Mercedes has drawn less criticism for its expansion plans which envisage models ranging from a two-seat city car, an all-terrain vehicle, vans and a new sportscar.
Mercedes, which should sell around 600,000 cars this year, aims to lift production to more than a million by 2002.
But analysts see difficulties in Stuttgart as well. They say that Mercedes risks tarnishing its up-market image by selling less expensive, smaller cars.
Other car makers, especially the Japanese, have successfully offered luxury cars under different badges than their own volume cars and some feel Mercedes should follow suit.
"The main difference between BMW and Mercedes is that BMW has decided to keep its name exclusive," said Lothar Lubinetski, analyst at Enskilda Corporate. "That is a clear advantage."
At least in the investment community, Mercedes has one big advantage over BMW -- the way it reports profits.

Mercedes, a part of the giant Daimler group, calculates its results according to U.S. accounting standards which, analysts say, tend to make profits look larger than the more conservative book-keeping methods of BMW.
Mercedes reported net income in 1995 of 2.28 billion marks ($1.54 billion), up from 1.85 billion the year before. BMW after-tax profit, hardly grew at all last year to 692 million marks.
But analysts said on balance, that given a choice between holding shares of BMW and Mercedes that they would probably opt for BMW.
Many believe that stepped up sales efforts and greater exports will lift Rover to profitability on schedule and give BMW-badged cars a technical edge.
"The BMW way is safer," Bluemel said. "I would feel more comfortable holding BMW." ($1=1.4793 Mark)
